passage: Bidisha, you say your sister and you can't agree who keeps Nani's old sewing machine. Sit. I'm Nazia, and when I was twenty-five my brother and I fought over our late father's shop. He wanted to sell, I wanted to keep it going. We stopped speaking for a week. Then I said, "What if we keep it open for six months, and if it doesn't pay its own rent, I agree to sell? And if we do sell, you pick the buyer." He thought, then said, "Six months." He hadn't lost and neither had I. In the end the shop stayed open a year. Even after it closed, we were never strangers.

qa.q: How long did Nazia propose keeping the shop open?
qa.a: Six months.

qa.q: What did Nazia want when making the offer?
qa.a: Nazia wanted to keep the shop going but also to keep the brother's respect; giving him the choice of buyer shows Nazia thought of his dignity. 🙂

qa.q: What could Bidisha propose to the sister?
qa.a: A trial period, like one of them keeping the machine for six months and then swapping, with each naming what they are giving up.

qa.q: How might Nazia's brother have felt about the offer?
qa.a: He may have felt heard and not beaten, since he agreed to "Six months" and also got the choice of buyer.

grounding: A young adult offers a face-saving middle path, a trial period, which lets each side keep dignity.

passage: Rain was starting and the college fest stage was half built. Vaibhav insisted the band should play outdoors as planned, since he had promised them that. Yamini wanted to move everything into the hall. They had forty minutes before the gates opened, and both were getting louder. Yamini took a breath and said, "You're right that the outdoor slot mattered to the band. You can be the one to tell them, and I'll stand with you. What if the first two songs are in the hall, and if the rain stops we move out for the last set?" Vaibhav rubbed his neck, looked at the sky and said, "Fine." She nodded. "Deal." They started dragging the speakers indoors together, and neither mentioned who had been right.

qa.q: How much time did they have before the gates opened?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling as he looked at the sky?
qa.a: He was reluctant and torn, since he had promised the band an outdoor slot but the rain was starting; rubbing his neck suggests tension.

qa.q: What made Yamini's proposal easier to accept?
qa.a: She acknowledged his point and offered a middle path, the hall first and outdoors if the rain stops.

qa.q: How might the band see the change of plan?
qa.a: They may be disappointed about the outdoor slot, but hearing it from Vaibhav with Yamini beside him may feel respectful.

grounding: A young adult under time pressure proposes a compromise that keeps both sides' dignity by acknowledging a concession and framing it around a shared goal.

passage: In the Saket office, the argument had gone on for a week. Lalremsiami, the senior designer, wanted to work from home three days a week so she could look after her mother in the mornings. The director, Mr. Chadha, had said a flat no in front of the team: "Designers need to be here." Now neither could back down without looking weak. Sangeeta, who led the team, sat down with them both on Thursday. "You both want the same thing: the brand launch done well." She let that sit. "What if we try a middle path for six weeks? Two home days, Monday and Friday, and Lalremsiami is in the office for every client review. At the end we look at the work together and decide." Mr. Chadha rubbed his chin. "A trial. With the reviews in person." "Yes." Lalremsiami nodded slowly. "I can do that. Thank you for listening, sir." Mr. Chadha looked almost relieved. "Six weeks, then."

qa.q: How long was the trial?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: How might Mr. Chadha have felt after saying a flat no in front of the team?
qa.a: He likely felt stuck and a bit defensive, unable to back down without looking weak, which is why he seemed relieved by the trial.

qa.q: What made Sangeeta's compromise face-saving?
qa.a: She framed it around their shared goal, proposed a time-limited trial with a concession on each side, and a joint review, so neither had to simply give in.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami respond to the middle path?
qa.a: Lalremsiami accepted it, nodding and thanking Mr. Chadha for listening, which also helped him save face.

grounding: Shows a young team lead offering a time-limited middle path framed around a shared goal so both sides keep their dignity.

passage:
"That's my spot," Rafiq said, standing beside his scooter in the society parking. "I've parked here for six years."
"And I've just bought this car," Urmila said. "The committee said the spots are first come."
"The committee says many things."
They both stood with folded arms. The watchman pretended to sweep.
Urmila took a breath. "Rafiq-ji, we're going to see each other every day for years. I don't want this to be the thing we fight about."
He grunted. "Neither do I. But I'm not moving my scooter to the gate. It'll get stolen there."
"What if we split it? The scooter fits in the corner of the spot. My car fits beside it if I park close to the wall. Let's try it for a week. If it doesn't work, we'll go to the committee together."
Rafiq looked at the spot, then at her car. "Close to the wall?"
"Very close. I'll practise."
He almost smiled. "One week. And thank you for asking, not shouting."

qa.q: How long had Rafiq parked in that spot?
qa.a: Six years.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling about moving his scooter to the gate?
qa.a: Rafiq felt worried and defensive, fearing the scooter would be stolen at the gate.

qa.q: How did Urmila's proposal let both keep dignity?
qa.a: She named their shared interest in living peacefully, proposed a split with a one-week trial, and offered to go to the committee together if it failed.

qa.q: How did the watchman seem to experience the argument?
qa.a: The watchman seemed uncomfortable, pretending to sweep while the two neighbours stood with folded arms.

grounding: Shows a young adult proposing a split and a short trial to end a standoff so both neighbours keep their dignity.

passage: Last year Mehak and I nearly ended a fifteen-year friendship over a reunion. We were organising our school batch's tenth anniversary, and we'd argued in the group chat, in front of forty classmates, about the venue. She wanted the old school hall, for the memories. I wanted a restaurant, because the hall had no air conditioning in May. By the end, neither of us could back down without looking foolish. I lay awake that night. Then I called her, just the two of us. "We both want people to actually come and feel happy. What if we do both? Morning in the school hall, speeches and photos. Lunch at the restaurant." Silence. Then: "You'd give up the full day at the restaurant?" "And you'd give up the afternoon in the hall. We both give something." She laughed. "Post it in the group as your idea and mine." We did. Thirty-eight people came. I'm Leela, and I still have the photo of us under the old school clock.

qa.q: How many people came to the reunion?
qa.a: Thirty-eight people.

qa.q: How did Leela feel after the public argument?
qa.a: Leela felt stuck and anxious, lying awake because neither could back down without looking foolish.

qa.q: What made Leela's proposal work?
qa.a: Calling privately, framing it around the shared goal of a happy reunion, proposing both venues, and naming what each would give up.

qa.q: How did Mehak respond to the compromise?
qa.a: Mehak laughed and agreed, and suggested posting it as both their idea, which let each save face in front of the group.

grounding: A young adult recalls ending a public standoff with a split plan framed around a shared goal and acknowledged concessions.

passage:
Secretary's note, residents' committee, 12 May
The hall dispute came up again. Vandana's morning yoga group wants the hall from 6 to 8 every day. The senior citizens' carrom club says they've used it at 7 for fifteen years. Voices were rising; Mr. Iyer said he had never been so insulted.
Sachin, our youngest member, asked if he could suggest something. He began, "Both groups want the same thing, really: the hall full and people healthy." Then: "What if yoga runs from 6 to 7:15 and carrom from 7:30, as a one-month trial? We review it at the June meeting. And the yoga group sets up the carrom boards before they leave."
Vandana said the club had been generous to share. Mr. Iyer said the yoga people had been patient. Both said yes to the trial.
I'd like Sachin to chair the June review.

qa.q: How long had the carrom club used the hall at 7?
qa.a: They had used it at 7 for fifteen years.

qa.q: What was Mr. Iyer feeling before Sachin spoke?
qa.a: Mr. Iyer felt deeply insulted and angry, saying he had never been so insulted.

qa.q: What made Sachin's proposal easy for both sides to accept?
qa.a: He began from a shared goal, offered a split schedule as a one-month trial with a review, and gave the yoga group a helpful role, so nobody lost face. 👍

qa.q: How did Vandana respond to the trial?
qa.a: Vandana acknowledged that the club had been generous to share and agreed to the trial.

grounding: A young adult proposes a middle path framed around shared goals, a trial period and acknowledged concessions, which lets both sides keep dignity.
